content: The introduction of complementary feeding during the early years of life is critical for establishing and maintaining the nutritional status of infants. Failure to introduce complementary feeding between 6 and 23 months of age can result in malnutrition. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends providing a variety of complementary foods, including fruits and vegetables, animal-source foods (ASF), and nuts, pulses, and seeds, to meet the nutritional demands of infants during this period of rapid growth and development. Among these, animal-source foods are particularly important as they are rich in both macroand micronutrients, provide high-quality proteins, and stimulate growth-promoting hormones in children. The purpose of this systematic review was to evaluate the health, developmental, and dietary effects of more frequent versus less frequent, greater versus lesser amounts, and more varied versus less varied consumption of ASF during the complementary feeding period. Additionally, the review aimed to compare the effects of processed/commercial ASF versus fresh/home-prepared ASF on dietary and health outcomes. The search strategy was developed using the PICO methodology and included searches in electronic databases such as MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, African Index Medicus, LILACS, Cochrane CENTRAL, and eLENA (WHO). Grey literature was also searched using Google Scholar, organizational websites, and reference lists of relevant systematic reviews. All search results were screened in duplicate, and individual studies were critically appraised using tools such as the Cochrane Risk of Bias-2 (ROB-2) tool for randomized controlled trials, the NIH tool for observational cohort and cross-sectional studies, and the ROBINS-I tool for non-randomized studies. GRADE certainty assessments were conducted for outcomes included in meta-analyses, such as stunting (HAZ), wasting (WAZ), underweight (WHZ), changes in head circumference, triceps skinfold thickness, and anemia or hemoglobin levels. The inclusion criteria for this review were studies involving healthy male and female children aged 6–23 months from any low-, middle-, or high-income country. The studies needed to report ASF consumption in terms of frequency, variety, or amount and measure primary or secondary outcomes of interest. Studies involving unhealthy child populations or qualitative studies were excluded. Data extraction and analysis were performed independently by four review authors, with disagreements resolved through discussion or by a third reviewer. Experimental and observational study data were analyzed separately. Meta-analysis was only feasible for three outcomes (WAZ, HAZ, WHZ) due to heterogeneity in food group items consumed, outcome metrics, and frequency categories. A narrative synthesis was conducted for all exposures and outcomes. The review included 31 studies analyzing data from 278,358 children aged 0–12 years at enrollment. These studies were conducted in Europe (n=9), Africa (n=7), Asia (n=5), North America (n=3), South America (n=1), and one multi-center study. Of these, 17 were observational studies, 15 were randomized experimental studies, and one was a non-randomized experimental study. Thirteen studies examined the frequency of ASF consumption, 18 examined the amount, and two examined the variety of ASF. Most outcomes were reported by single studies, limiting the ability to draw definitive conclusions about the effects of different frequencies, amounts, and varieties of ASF consumption. Regarding the frequency of ASF consumption, no randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs were identified. Observational studies showed no significant differences in outcomes between greater and lesser amounts of ASF consumption, with GRADE ratings ranging from very low to moderate. However, a significant 48% reduction in wasting was observed among children who consumed fish ≥4 times per week compared to those who consumed fish 1–3 times per week (GRADE = moderate). For the amount of ASF consumed, no differences in growth and nutritional outcomes were found among children given different types of meat, including red meat, organ meat, pork, eggs, dairy, seafood, and insects. Two studies that measured different amounts of ASF were meta-analyzed for WAZ, HAZ, and WHZ outcomes. In one study, children aged 6–9 months were followed for six months after being given one egg per day versus no egg consumption, showing moderate-quality evidence of benefits. Another study assessed the impact of varying amounts of cow’s milk on hemoglobin, serum ferritin, transferrin receptors, and mean corpuscular volume, finding no significant differences (GRADE = very low for hemoglobin). Regarding the variety of ASF, no RCTs or quasi-RCTs were identified. Observational studies reported no significant differences in stunting among children consuming three types of ASF versus two types, or two types versus one type. However, a potential 1% reduction in stunting was observed in children consuming one type of ASF compared to those consuming none (GRADE = very low). Overall, the quality of observational studies was rated as good for two studies, fair for nine studies, and poor for six studies. For randomized experimental studies, one study was rated as high risk of bias, nine as moderate risk, and three as low risk. The single non-randomized experimental study was rated as low to moderate risk of bias. The findings of this systematic review aim to inform the development of updated WHO infant and young child feeding guidelines, as well as country-specific policies and programs related to complementary feeding. However, the high heterogeneity among studies limited the ability to conduct meta-analyses for most outcomes. Only three outcomes (WAZ, HAZ, WHZ) from two studies were meta-analyzed, with GRADE ratings of low to moderate. This review highlights significant data gaps in the evidence and quality of studies, emphasizing the need for more consistent and higher-quality research to enable pooled findings and the development of appropriate guidelines. Adequate nutrition during infancy is essential for a child’s full developmental potential later in life. The first two years of life are critical for physical and cognitive growth, and poor dietary intake during this period can lead to increased morbidity, mortality, and delayed motor and mental development in the short term. In the long term, poor nutrition can impair intellectual performance, work capacity, reproductive health, and overall health outcomes, resulting in significant loss of human capital. Complementary feeding during the formative years is crucial for building and maintaining the nutritional status of infants, as failure to introduce complementary feeding can lead to malnutrition. Malnutrition in children includes both undernutrition (stunting and wasting) and overnutrition (overweight and obesity), often associated with micronutrient deficiencies. Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended until six months of age, after which complementary feeding should be initiated alongside breast milk to meet the increasing nutritional demands of the growing infant. Complementary foods can be specially prepared or modified family foods. While breastfeeding may continue beyond two years, complementary feeding is typically targeted to infants aged 6–23 months, after which they are expected to consume family foods. Despite the benefits of continued breastfeeding, there is less consensus on aspects of complementary feeding, such as timing, patterns of introduction, and the amount and frequency of different food types. Animal-source foods are particularly important during complementary feeding as they provide nutrients not readily available from plant-based foods, such as vitamin A, vitamin B12, calcium, zinc, iron, and riboflavin. Reduced intake of these nutrients can lead to anemia, growth abnormalities, cognitive decline, neuromuscular issues, and even death. Studies have shown that children consuming less ASF during infancy are at increased risk of stunting, while those given ASF demonstrate better growth and cognitive outcomes. Additionally, maternal consumption of ASF during pregnancy benefits the fetus by breaking the intergenerational cycle of undernutrition. Proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals from ASF, such as eggs, are essential for children’s growth and development. For example, a study in rural Burkina Faso found that infants given eggs in their complementary diet had lower incidences of wasting and underweight. Another study reported that protein from ASF is positively associated with infant growth.
